opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in the field right now. There's a tendency to assume that if you have a big enough network and enough data, generalization will just take care of itself. But the expressive power of your representation fundamentally shapes what you can learn efficiently, and from how much data.

Here's the way I think about it. Deep networks are essentially circuits. A circuit is a very weak representation language in a certain sense. It can't express general rules compactly. Take the rules of Go. In first-order logic or a simple program you can write them in about a page: for any board position, for any location, a stone is captured if this condition holds. A circuit has no quantifiers, so it has to represent those rules more or less separately for every location and every configuration. That means an enormous number of parameters and an enormous amount of data to learn something that, in a more expressive language, is quite simple.

We actually see the consequences of this. Some of the superhuman Go programs turned out to have failed to learn the concept of a group of stones correctly. An amateur could beat them with a fairly simple strategy, because the networks had learned a patchwork approximation rather than the actual concept. That's a fingerprint of a representation that can't express the general rule, so it covers the cases it has seen and fails in ways no human would.

So my view is that effective generalization comes from representations that can express things compactly: first-order logic, probabilistic programs, programming languages in general. The fundamental principle of learning is that if you can describe your hypothesis more concisely, you need less data to pin it down. If the true regularity in the world is simple in an expressive language but horribly complicated in your language, you pay for that mismatch in data and in brittleness.

That's not to say deep learning has no role. It's extraordinarily good at certain perceptual tasks. But I don't think scaling circuits alone gets us to robust, human-like generalization. I suspect what we'll need is some combination where the system can build and reason with structured, expressive models of the world: objects, relations, causal structure, with learning operating over those richer representations. That was much of the motivation behind our work on probabilistic programming languages like BLOG: you want the expressiveness of first-order logic and the ability to handle uncertainty that probability theory gives you, together.

r001.rationale: The candidate argues that effective generalization benefits from expressive representations such as first-order logic and programming languages; it does not state that those are often unnecessary.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses Go rules and circuits, but does not mention implementing a probabilistic context-free grammar parser or compare the difficulty of doing so in a programming language versus a circuit.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the oldest questions in the field, and it's one we keep rediscovering. If you go back to the early days, people were working with propositional representations, essentially feature vectors, and the problem was always that you needed an enormous number of examples to learn anything, because each new situation looked like a completely different pattern. You couldn't say "for all objects, if X then Y." You had to learn it separately for every object.

So my view has long been that generalization depends on having a representation that can express the regularities that actually exist in the world. And the world is full of objects and relations and quantification. There are many things, they stand in relationships to each other, and the rules that govern them apply universally. If your hypothesis space can't express "every king is in check when attacked by an unobstructed piece," then you're going to be learning that fact over and over for each square on the board. That's where first-order logic and probabilistic programming come from. They let you write down knowledge that's compact precisely because it's general.

Now, the deep learning community has taken a very different approach. They've essentially said: don't worry about expressive representations, just use a huge circuit and lots of data. And it works astonishingly well in many cases. But I'd argue it works because of scale that papers over the lack of expressiveness. Circuits are, at bottom, propositional. They don't have variables in the logical sense. So when you see large language models failing to generalize, say, from arithmetic on five-digit numbers to arithmetic on eight-digit numbers, or playing Go at superhuman level and then losing to a strategy a decent amateur could recognize, that's exactly the symptom I'd expect. The system has learned a vast number of special cases rather than the underlying rule.

So I'd put it this way: the expressive power you need is roughly the expressive power of the regularities you're trying to capture. If the world has universal laws, you need universals. If it has uncertainty, you need probability. If it has objects that persist and interact, you need some notion of object and relation. We know how to combine these things in principle, in probabilistic first-order languages, and the challenge is making learning and inference tractable there. I think that's a far more promising route to robust generalization than just hoping the next order of magnitude of compute fixes the problem.

r001.rationale: The response argues that robust generalization needs representations expressive enough to capture the world’s regularities, including universals, probability, objects, and relations. It does not state that effective generalization often needs less than the full expressive power of programming languages or first-order logic.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention implementing a probabilistic context-free grammar parser or compare how easy it is to implement one in a programming language versus directly as a circuit.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that generalization depends on the language in which you can express what you’ve learned. If your representation is too limited, something that ought to be a simple general rule may require an enormous collection of separate examples.

Think about learning that objects persist when you’re not looking at them. You want to express that as a rule about objects, rather than separately learning it for every object, in every location, from every possible viewpoint. So having objects, relations, and variables in your representation gives you a way to state knowledge that applies to situations you’ve never encountered.

Now, expressive power by itself isn’t enough. A very expressive language also gives you an enormous space of possible explanations, and you need ways to find the right ones. But I think it’s a mistake to suppose that restricting the representation necessarily makes learning easier. Sometimes a richer representation makes the underlying explanation much simpler—and that’s precisely what allows you to generalize.

r001.rationale: The response argues that richer expressive power can support generalization, but never says that full programming-language or first-order-logic expressiveness is unnecessary.

r002.rationale: It does not mention probabilistic context-free grammar parsers, programming-language implementation, or circuit implementation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish expressive power from the ability to learn. A system might be able to represent an enormously complicated function, but that doesn’t tell you whether it can find the right function from a reasonable amount of experience.

One of the advantages of a language with objects and relations is that it lets you express general rules very compactly. If I say that objects fall when you let go of them, I’m not making a separate statement about every object I’ve ever seen. I’m making a statement that applies to objects I haven’t seen, too. That’s a very powerful kind of generalization.

And this is why I’m interested in combining expressive representations with probability and learning. You want to represent the structure of the world, but you also want to be uncertain about it and revise your beliefs as evidence comes in. The challenge is to get that expressiveness while keeping learning and inference computationally manageable.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes representational expressive power from the ability to learn and gives a compact general rule, but does not say that effective generalization often needs less than the full power of programming languages or first-order logic.
